newsitem.title: FRANCE: French drug stocks active on bid speculation.
newsitem.headline: French drug stocks active on bid speculation.

text.p: Shares in French pharmaceutical companies were active on Friday on merger speculation after Elf-Aquitaine put its Sanofi drug unit in play.
The activity was also bolstered by arbitrage in the sector prompted by a buyout by Hoechst of the minority shareholders in Roussel-Uclaf, brokers said.
Sanofi shares were up 4.66 percent at 517 francs at 1110 GMT after their 6.24 percent gain on Thursday. Elf shares rose 2.66 percent to 467.70 francs after gaining 4.54 percent the previous day.
Roussel-Uclaf shares were up 5.7 percent on Friday -- the first day of Hoechst's buyout operation.
"Roussel-Uclaf will be delisted. Investors in the share are shifting to other stocks in the sector," a trader said.

Shares in Rhone-Poulenc, which has agreed to merge its animal health activities with those of Merck & Co, were 3.16 percent higher at 173 francs even though the company said on Thursday it was not interested in a pharmaceutical alliance.

But a market specialist said Rhone was nonetheless benefitting more from the speculation than Synthelabo, two-thirds owned by cosmetics giant L'Oreal, or Sanofi, "which are quite expensive at these levels".
Shares in Synthelabo were up 2.55 percent at 563 francs. Analysts speculated that Britain's Zeneca or Warner Lambert Co might make good partners for the firm.
L'Oreal has long refuted recurring talk that it may sell its controlling stake in Synthelabo, saying it has been a good investment.
L'Oreal declined to comment on the latest speculation, which rose a notch on Thursday after Elf said it was willing to sell control of Sanofi if the subsidiary found a merger partner.

Most analysts rule out a Synthelabo-Sanofi pairing, saying it would not help Sanofi attain its goal of expanding in the United States. But one analyst said Synthelabo's strong presence in Japan might look tempting to Sanofi.
Some analysts say Bristol-Myers Squibb, which cooperates with Sanofi to develop some medicines, may be a better partner for the French firm.

But one analyst said there may be resistance in France to a a foreign takeover of a company in the pharmaceutical sector -- an industry prized by public authorities and slated to get special protection in anti-takeover legislation being drafted.
